      "markdown": "# Beyond code generation: remote control, security review and runtime inspection
As of: 2026-10-15

**Visual direction:** Opening title card for Google Vids or HeyGen. Plan for synthetic narration, with a visible disclosure: “AI-generated narration.” Show three labeled icons: remote interaction, security review, runtime inspection. All interface diagrams should be labeled illustrative, not product demonstrations.

**Narration:** This presentation uses an AI-generated voice. As of October 15, 2026, some concrete AI coding developments extend beyond writing code. They offer ways to supervise an agent remotely, request security findings, and inspect running software. For someone building a small app or script alone, those are capabilities worth investigating. They are not evidence that a project can now finish itself.

**Visual direction:** Connect a phone icon to a laptop. Keep the agent icon inside the laptop. Add “Computer must stay on and online.”

**Narration:** First, Cursor announced that its iOS app can display local agents and let you message them. Here, an agent means the assistant carrying out development work. The important distinction is where that work happens: it still runs on your computer. The phone connects to it; it does not move the task into cloud execution. Your computer must remain on and online. That gives you another way to interact with ongoing work, not a different place for the work to run.

[01-c1] [Cursor: Remote control for local agents](https://cursor.com/changelog/remote-control-local-agents "item_id=feed:86e64baebef7f0e23a96adbb; version_id=f0b87f5852d125e85cbeb2438fe5d0ee73e1a1bface9f1ea7031804286fb5ea1")

**Visual direction:** Show a review card with three fields: severity, attack path, proposed fix. Add access labels: “Teams / Enterprise” and “Draft pull requests skipped.”

**Narration:** Second, Cursor announced Security Review for selected repositories. Its advertised findings contain a severity, an attack path, and a proposed fix. An attack path describes how the reported problem could be reached or exploited. Draft pull requests are skipped, and access is offered on Teams and Enterprise plans. For an individual developer, eligibility and purchase practicality therefore matter. The announcement establishes the proposed review format and access restrictions. It does not establish how effectively the tool detects vulnerabilities.

[01-c2] [Cursor: Rollouts and Security Review](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer "item_id=feed:50257040989ddf36da8c107e; version_id=126e7b7700183bbf6dfce1990231a8f468e9de35c1f6ac20a396cd30d761b08c")

**Visual direction:** Show an illustrative flame graph and source heatmap, labeled “Runtime inspection—not a measured speedup.” Do not invent profiling measurements.

**Narration:** Third, Simon Willison reports having Codex run Python 3.15’s profiler against his web-edit application, producing a flame graph and heatmap. A profiler helps inspect where execution spends time. This is a concrete example of assistant-assisted debugging and inspection. But producing a profile is not the same as demonstrating an optimization, and his account does not measure a delivery-time saving or the full cost of testing and correction.

[01-c3] [Willison: Profiling web-edit with Python 3.15](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/ "item_id=feed:26e4a943393a1b788d1e2dae; version_id=de47f3a642088f8a087f0a6f46b95b49b6830aa108fd56ccd1dec0cf490cb5f8")

**Visual direction:** Contrast a green “Job completed” badge with an empty review panel. Then show “Inspect the delivered result.”

**Narration:** GitHub’s October availability report supplies a useful counterweight. Describing its September 28 Copilot code-review incident, GitHub says some jobs reported successful completion without delivering a review. It says it reverted the change and advised customers to request affected reviews again. A completion signal, in other words, was not proof that the expected output existed.

[01-c4] [GitHub: September 2026 availability report](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-september-2026/ "item_id=feed:5942317efb2e306a353cac42; version_id=2b8477c36458d01b02ef31fabffdfe1ae8339b51ac8a1407d7819528f05c4151")

**Visual direction:** End with three checkboxes: actual changes, delivered review, runtime profile. Below them: “Broader actions ≠ proven productivity gain.”

**Narration:** The practical takeaway is to judge these developments by inspectable results: actual agent changes, a delivered review, or a runtime profile. We still do not know whether these capabilities improve completion rates for typical small solo projects. Cursor and GitHub describe products they sell; Willison describes his own application. None provides independent, representative evidence about beginners, abandoned projects, or accessibility users. Broader development actions are the concrete change. Verified outcomes should remain your acceptance criterion.

[01-c5] [Cursor remote interaction](https://cursor.com/changelog/remote-control-local-agents), [Willison’s profiling artifact](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/), and [GitHub’s missing-review account](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-availability-report-september-2026/).",

      "piece_id": "02",
      "markdown": "# Review activity is not the same as verified correctness
As of: 2026-10-15

**Visual direction:** Opening title card for Google Vids or HeyGen. Plan for synthetic narration and display “AI-generated narration.” Introduce a three-stage diagram: criticism → checked defect → checked repair. Keep the arrows visually separate.

**Narration:** This presentation uses an AI-generated voice. As of October 15, 2026, the evidence around AI code review supports a narrow conclusion: tools can produce criticism, benchmarks can assess review tasks, and developers can experiment with another model as a reviewer. None of those facts, by itself, proves that a defect was confirmed or correctly repaired. For a solo developer, that distinction matters more than the number of comments generated.

**Visual direction:** Display “ReviewBench: 219 pull requests / 187 repositories / 19 languages.” Beside it, show “Tiny, single-file changes deliberately reduced.” Do not illustrate these figures as performance scores.

**Narration:** Consider GitHub’s ReviewBench. GitHub describes it as containing 219 pull requests from 187 public, open-source-licensed repositories across 19 languages. A pull request is a proposed code change submitted for review. The benchmark deliberately reduces the representation of tiny, single-file changes in favor of more substantial, multi-file work. That makes its task mix important to examine before applying results to the small edits common in individual projects. Inspectable tasks are useful, but their relevance to your work still needs checking.

[02-c1] [GitHub: ReviewBench](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-ai-code-review/ "item_id=feed:9e3099b85951738510dd7533; version_id=754cbbbbef0fdf63f52b8ef6428375ee7418da83b3001588ad78d50c265ee276")

**Visual direction:** Animate “Review comment → code change,” then pause before a separate “Confirmed defect removed” box. Label the first arrow “LLM-inferred response.”

**Narration:** Next, look closely at the metric. GitHub defines addressed rate as the percentage of review comments that a language model judges to have prompted a corresponding code change. That is an inferred developer response. It is not independent verification that a defect existed or that the edit removed it. GitHub also acknowledges that a fixed set of expected findings becomes incomplete as systems discover issues its creators did not anticipate. Both qualifications matter when interpreting review scores.

[02-c2] [GitHub: addressed rate and expected-findings limitations](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-ai-code-review/)

**Visual direction:** Show two generic reviewer cards labeled Claude and GPT, pointing toward the same code change. Caption: “Reported practice; effectiveness not measured here.”

**Narration:** Simon Willison reports trying adversarial review in his own projects: asking a model to look for flaws, sometimes playing Claude and GPT against each other. This establishes an attributed practice, not a measured improvement in defect detection. His account does not provide a review-cost comparison or artifacts that establish its effectiveness.

[02-c3] [Willison: Redesigning source control at Anthropic](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/redesigning-source-control-at-anthropic/ "item_id=feed:f4e5f15fa292a88ed95d2678; version_id=817db9b58ff0b94efe6611d6718fc6c85e481aaa12ddceefd0cfe548a24f4c1f")

**Visual direction:** Show “Advertised targets” above injection, authentication bypass, and authorization bypass. Place severity, attack path, and proposed fix underneath as output fields.

**Narration:** Cursor, meanwhile, says Security Review looks for injection and bypasses of authentication or authorization checks. Its findings include an attack path and proposed fix. Those are advertised targets and output fields, not evidence of how many real vulnerabilities it finds or misses. The supplied announcement contains no detection evaluation.

[02-c4] [Cursor: Security Review](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer "item_id=feed:50257040989ddf36da8c107e; version_id=126e7b7700183bbf6dfce1990231a8f468e9de35c1f6ac20a396cd30d761b08c")

**Visual direction:** Return to the opening diagram. Highlight “Check relevance” and “Check behavior” between criticism and confirmation.

**Narration:** Treat AI criticism as a candidate finding until you check its relevance and behavior. We cannot infer verified correctness from a comment, an edit, or agreement between reviewers. GitHub built its benchmark with Microsoft and evaluates a product it sells; its separate relabeling used internal senior engineers, not an independent publisher. Experienced practitioners may also be better equipped than beginners to reject plausible but irrelevant criticism. These sources address different stages of review. The unresolved step is confirming the defect and checking the repair.

[02-c5] [GitHub’s response metric](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/reviewbench-an-open-benchmark-for-ai-code-review/), [Willison’s experimental practice](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/redesigning-source-control-at-anthropic/), [Cursor’s advertised findings](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer), and [GitHub’s researcher interview: confirm findings yourself](https://github.blog/security/how-one-bug-bounty-researcher-chooses-the-features-they-investigate/ "item_id=feed:c15f6182059e3b795d1a52ce; version_id=c410af6157583580b670a5f6d145915c7bbb8485b3a7de9cc4d75e6fccc35893").",

      "piece_id": "03",
      "markdown": "# Try one bounded task—and account for the work needed to verify it
As of: 2026-10-15

**Visual direction:** Opening title card for Google Vids or HeyGen. Plan for synthetic narration, displaying “AI-generated narration.” Show one task card inside a boundary, with an undo arrow and a checklist.

**Narration:** This presentation uses an AI-generated voice. As of October 15, 2026, a defensible next step with AI coding assistance is one small, reversible trial—not immediate adoption of a more elaborate agent workflow. Choose a repository convention or debugging question, define what would count as success, and inspect the result. These are proposed checks, not a tested recipe or a promise of faster delivery.

**Visual direction:** Show the exact path `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. Beside it, place “One convention” and “Explicit validation commands.” Avoid inventing project-specific commands.

**Narration:** Start with context you can inspect. GitHub’s tutorial recommends adding repository guidance in a file called copilot-instructions dot md inside the dot github directory. Its advice is to choose one convention you keep explaining and observe how Copilot applies it to the next task. Include explicit validation commands rather than adopting every customization at once. Treat the instructions as guidance to check, not an enforced guarantee that the assistant will follow them.

[03-c1] [GitHub: How to teach Copilot about your codebase](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/github-copilot-app-for-beginners-how-to-teach-copilot-about-your-codebase/ "item_id=feed:f8fa0331a2b3ce4696b878a2; version_id=a0ac872c91e89fad8413b83b3c5683bf89c547a0fcc88f0f3f56d7645592e8a3")

**Visual direction:** Show a main-thread lane and a worker-thread lane. Highlight “95.1% of recorded stacks: AnyIO worker thread,” explicitly attributed to Willison’s example. Add “Sample frequency is not elapsed-time saving.”

**Narration:** For a performance question, the verification setup itself matters. Simon Willison reports that 95.1 percent of recorded stacks in his web-edit profiling example came from AnyIO’s worker thread. A main-thread-only profile would have missed them. Sampling periodically captures snapshots of execution. Before comparing an assistant’s proposed change, reproduce a relevant workload and include the threads doing the work. Sample frequencies alone do not establish elapsed-time savings. Python version compatibility and permission requirements also need checking.

[03-c2] [Willison: web-edit profiling](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/ "item_id=feed:26e4a943393a1b788d1e2dae; version_id=de47f3a642088f8a087f0a6f46b95b49b6830aa108fd56ccd1dec0cf490cb5f8"); [Willison: Python 3.15 sampling profiler and permissions](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/12/python-3-15/ "item_id=feed:dbe23f001a073722b9cecf6d; version_id=66c209040e72efd8fe6b6b823e1b16a0e93bffccf043a92d8341425e631936fe")

**Visual direction:** Use a conditional flow: access and price checked → authorized test copy → reproduce reported behavior → check fix and intended use. Label it “Evaluation, not adoption recommendation.”

**Narration:** For security review, first check access and price. Cursor’s announced tool is offered on Teams and Enterprise plans, so practicality for an individual remains unresolved. If a trial is accessible, use an authorized test copy. Try to reproduce the reported attack path, then check whether the proposed fix removes that behavior without breaking intended use. This is a conditional evaluation, not a recommendation to buy or adopt the tool.

[03-c3] [Cursor: access and finding format](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer "item_id=feed:50257040989ddf36da8c107e; version_id=126e7b7700183bbf6dfce1990231a8f468e9de35c1f6ac20a396cd30d761b08c"); [GitHub researcher interview: verify findings](https://github.blog/security/how-one-bug-bounty-researcher-chooses-the-features-they-investigate/ "item_id=feed:c15f6182059e3b795d1a52ce; version_id=c410af6157583580b670a5f6d145915c7bbb8485b3a7de9cc4d75e6fccc35893")

**Visual direction:** Show two attributed experience cards, not a comparative performance chart: “Mostly short tasks; no further limit after switching back” and “Combined workflows; usage exhausted.”

**Narration:** Budget usage before chaining steps together. The HTML All The Things hosts describe different experiences. One reports mostly short tasks and no further limit after switching back to another model. The other describes combining shorter steps into longer workflows and exhausting usage. These are practitioner accounts, not a controlled comparison or evidence that one model is superior. They do not establish an ideal task size.

[03-c4] [HTML All The Things: AI’s Biggest Problem Isn’t Intelligence Anymore](https://www.htmlallthethings.com/podcast/ais-biggest-problem-isnt-intelligence-anymore "item_id=podcast:acc83661b4084b701efe6573; version_id=d30ec05b567a9c16691e94f84c0c309050357ceea62781c3afa91b62697aed23; segment_id=s00076; segment_id=s00078; segment_id=s00081; segment_id=s00131; segment_id=s00132; segment_id=s00136")

**Visual direction:** End on a blank trial record with fields: acceptance checks, delivered outputs, retries, quota/API spending, human testing time, correction time. Caption: “Measure verified delivery—not generation alone.”

**Narration:** Record your acceptance checks, delivered outputs, retries, quota or API spending, and human testing and correction time. Review that record before expanding the workflow. We do not know whether a second reviewer or paid security tool will repay its setup cost for your project. Commercial sources and experienced practitioners have limits as evidence for beginners. If your project lacks useful tests, building verification may itself be substantial work. Measure the cost of verified completion, not generation alone.

[03-c5] [GitHub’s incremental setup guidance](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/github-copilot-app-for-beginners-how-to-teach-copilot-about-your-codebase/), [verification guidance](https://github.blog/security/how-one-bug-bounty-researcher-chooses-the-features-they-investigate/), [Willison on goal-level usage costs](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/13/llm-gemini/ "item_id=feed:6ff0735dfa2a1786602e7b58; version_id=a6cb93a068bca6b88086500d4f84badfd6255baa823a198066b04d6a8e160110"), [reported usage pressure](https://www.htmlallthethings.com/podcast/ais-biggest-problem-isnt-intelligence-anymore "segment_id=s00136"), and [Cursor’s finding format](https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer).",
